title: Cap. 7 Quartum: sufficienter / efficaciter—death for elect by absolute saving will
latin: Quartum argumentum nobis praebebit receptissima illa inter omnes Theologos distinctio, qua dici solet, Christum pro omnibus mortuum fuisse sufficienter, pro electis mortuum efficaciter. Nam sicuti ex priore membro refutavimus illorum sententiam, qui negant Christi mortem ex decreto Dei esse omnibus hominibus remedium applicabile, ita ex hoc posteriore illi sunt refutandi, qui negant Christi mortem, idque ex decreto Dei, esse remedium electis efficaciter & infallibiliter applicandum. Quis enim potest esse alius sensus horum verborum, Mortuus est pro electis efficaciter, quam, Mortuus est absoluta intentione & efficaci voluntate servandi electos?
pass_a_gloss: A fourth argument will furnish us that most received distinction among all Theologians, by which it is customarily said that Christ died for all sufficiently, for the elect efficaciously. For just as from the former member we refuted the opinion of those who deny that the death of Christ by the decree of God is for all human beings an applicable remedy, so from this latter those are to be refuted who deny that the death of Christ, and that by the decree of God, is a remedy to be applied to the elect efficaciously and infallibly. For what other sense can there be of these words, He died for the elect efficaciously, than, He died with an absolute intention and efficacious will of saving the elect?
pass_b: A fourth argument is the distinction most received among all theologians: that Christ died for all sufficiently, for the elect efficaciously. Just as from the first half we refuted those who deny that Christ’s death, by God’s decree, is an applicable remedy for all people, so from the second half those must be refuted who deny that Christ’s death, and that by God’s decree, is a remedy to be applied to the elect efficaciously and infallibly. What else can “He died for the elect efficaciously” mean than that he died with an absolute intention and efficacious will to save the elect?

title: Cap. 7 Quartum: not contingent human will—Suarez on intended efficacy
latin: Nam si quis eo torqueat hanc distinctionem, quasi sensus esset, Mortem Christi, quae sufficiens est pro omnibus, in eventu efficacem fieri aliquibus ex contingente actu arbitrii humani; Primo, ipsis verbis refellitur: siquidem, quando dicitur, Christus mortuus est efficaciter pro his aut illis, denotamus singularem efficaciam ex voluntate speciali morientis profluentem, non ex contingente actu credentis dimanantem. Secundo, ab ipsis Jesuitis haec efficacia (ut ita loquar) eventualis non intelligitur in hac distinctione, sed efficacia ab ipso moriente specialiter intenta & promerita. Sic Suarez, In 3. disp. 41. pag. 629. Christus non meruit omnibus remissionem peccatorum quoad efficaciam, quia non applicavit suum meritum, ut omnes infallibiliter talem effectum consequerentur. Mereri igitur efficaciter vel quoad efficaciam est, ea intentione suum meritum applicare aliquibus personis, ut infallibiliter inde effectum vitae aeternae consequantur. Paulo planius, pag. 635. Meritums Christi aequaliter se habet ad omnes quoad sufficientiam, non quoad efficaciam. Quod intelligendum est non tantum in effectibus, qui in uno sit & non in alio, sed etiam ex parte voluntatis, qua Christus ipse diverso modo obtulit sua merita pro diversis. Denique illa omnia testimonia Scripturarum, quae mortem Christi nobis proponunt complicatam cum certo proposito redimendi suas oves, Filios Dei congregandi, Ecclesiam acquirendi, populum peculiarem mundandi & servandi, atque id genus alia a nobis supra commemorata, aperte demonstrant hanc efficaciam de qua loquuntur Theologi, a voluntate morientis Christi esse arcessendam, non ex contingente actu arbitrii humani petendam. Christus speciali quadam intentione oblationis suae impetravit ut electis efficax redderetur; non autem electi in aliqua apprehensione ex libero arbitrio evagante eam sibi reddiderunt efficacem.
pass_a_gloss: For if anyone twists this distinction that way, as if the sense were that the death of Christ, which is sufficient for all, becomes efficacious in the event for some from a contingent act of human free choice; First, it is refuted by the words themselves: seeing that, when it is said, Christ died efficaciously for these or those, we denote a singular efficacy flowing from the special will of the one dying, not issuing from a contingent act of the believer. Secondly, by the Jesuits themselves this (so to speak) eventual efficacy is not understood in this distinction, but efficacy specially intended and merited by the dying one himself. So Suarez, On 3, disp. 41, p. 629: Christ did not merit for all the remission of sins as to efficacy, because he did not apply his merit so that all would infallibly obtain such an effect. To merit therefore efficaciously or as to efficacy is, with that intention, to apply his merit to certain persons so that they may infallibly obtain therefrom the effect of eternal life. A little more plainly, p. 635: The merit of Christ stands equally toward all as to sufficiency, not as to efficacy. Which is to be understood not only in the effects, which are in one and not in another, but also on the part of the will, by which Christ himself offered his merits in a diverse mode for diverse persons. Finally all those testimonies of the Scriptures which set before us the death of Christ joined with a certain purpose of redeeming his sheep, of gathering the sons of God, of acquiring the Church, of cleansing and saving a peculiar people, and things of that kind commemorated by us above, openly demonstrate that this efficacy of which the Theologians speak is to be fetched from the will of the dying Christ, not sought from a contingent act of human free choice. Christ by a certain special intention of his offering obtained that it would be rendered efficacious for the elect; but the elect did not in some apprehension wandering from free choice render it efficacious for themselves.
pass_b: If someone twists the distinction as if Christ’s death, sufficient for all, became efficacious for some only by a contingent act of human free choice, the words themselves refute him: “Christ died efficaciously for these or those” marks a singular efficacy flowing from the dying one’s special will, not from the believer’s contingent act. Second, even the Jesuits do not take “efficacy” in this distinction as mere eventual efficacy, but as efficacy specially intended and merited by the dying one himself. So Suarez (On 3, disp. 41, p. 629): Christ did not merit remission of sins for all as to efficacy, because he did not apply his merit so that all would infallibly gain that effect. To merit efficaciously is to apply his merit to certain persons with the intention that they infallibly obtain eternal life from it. More plainly (p. 635): Christ’s merit stands equally toward all as to sufficiency, not as to efficacy—understood not only in the effects (in one, not another) but also in the will by which Christ offered his merits differently for different persons. Scripture’s witnesses that join Christ’s death to a sure purpose of redeeming his sheep, gathering God’s sons, acquiring the Church, and cleansing a peculiar people show that the efficacy theologians speak of is drawn from the dying Christ’s will, not from contingent free choice. By a special intention in his offering Christ obtained that it be made efficacious for the elect; the elect did not make it efficacious for themselves by some free-choice apprehension.
